To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the immune response against tumor antigens can hamper tumor growth; (2) the immune response is effective in preventing tumor growth in the preclinical phase; (3) the immune response can be induced by vaccination with the tumor antigen; (4) the tumor antigens that can be used for cancer immunopreventive vaccines are those recognized both by antibodies (i.e., they can be used in serological assays) and by T cells.

(i) the immune system can effectively hamper tumor progression at early stages of cancer; (ii) the identification of tumor antigens fulfilling the above-mentioned conditions is crucial for the development both of cancer immunoprophylaxis and of immunotherapy of MHC-loss tumors; and (iii) the immune system is capable of recognizing and eliminating MHC-loss tumor cells, thus providing new targets for the immunotherapy of advanced tumors.

(i) we have identified a novel antigen (TROP2) that fulfills the criteria for cancer immunopreventive vaccination; (ii) TROP2 is expressed by a large fraction of human cancers and its overexpression correlates with poor survival; and (iii) TROP2 can be targeted by both antibodies and T cells and can induce an immune response in vivo.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of novel tumor-associated antigens that can be recognized by the immune system and that could be exploited for immunotherapy and tumor immunoprevention.
the identification of new tumor antigens and the development of novel immunotherapies.
the identification of novel tumor-specific antigens that are suitable candidates for the development of preventive and therapeutic vaccines.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the development of a successful tumor immunoprevention strategy requires the identification of tumor antigens that are both pathogenetically relevant for tumor progression and recognizable by the immune response.
the field of tumor immunology is still in its infancy, with many challenges to be faced in the near future.
tumor antigens should be considered as a target for both tumor immunoprevention and immunotherapy.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the immune system can effectively hamper preclinical stages of the tumor progression.

we identified a novel tumor antigen, the tumor-associated antigen (TAA)-1, which fulfills these two conditions and which we have now successfully targeted in a preclinical model of cancer immunoprotection.
we identified a number of tumor-associated antigens that could be useful for immunotherapy and immunoprevention of cancer.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the immune system is not only able to recognize tumor antigens but is also able to track them down in tumor variants.
the immune system has the capacity to control the progression of preneoplastic lesions, but the immune response to tumor antigens may not always be sufficient.
the identification of novel antigens is a prerequisite for the development of new immunopreventive strategies and that the immune response can be effectively harnessed to prevent tumor growth.
